rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at mid temperature to elute all 8 compounds if possible and map the full elution window without an excessive truncation risk. This gives a first read on whether the sample is compressed early, spread across the gradient, or still retaining into the hold.

All peaks eluted within a narrow effective solvent window, so trim the gradient around that window to spend gradient time where the compounds actually elute and improve selectivity near the critical 4/5 pair. Keep tG and T unchanged to isolate the effect of narrowing the phi window.

The narrow-window run created new crowding, so revert to the broad window and test slope directly by doubling tG. If the critical pair is slope-sensitive, this should improve its resolution while keeping all compounds within the gradient.

The critical pair is clearly slope-sensitive because tG=40 fully resolved all pairs; now shorten from 40 toward the minimum tG that still keeps every pair at or above 1.5. A step to 24 min should retain most of the gained resolution while reducing t_last toward the no-penalty region.

The threshold for full resolution lies between 24 and 40 min, so test an intermediate slope closer to the likely boundary. This should show whether we can get all pairs to at least 1.5 while keeping the time penalty smaller than at 40 min.

Since slope alone trades one critical pair against another, probe temperature as the orthogonal lever most likely to change selectivity and possibly separate the close pair around rows 4/5 without needing a long gradient. Dropping to 25 C should increase retention modestly while revealing whether the critical overlaps are temperature-sensitive.

At 25 C only one pair remains slightly under-resolved, so make the smallest slope-softening change to push that pair over 1.5 while minimizing added time. This directly tests whether full resolution is reachable near the current optimum with only a small time penalty.

Since 25 C nearly resolves everything and 40 C changes the critical selectivity strongly, test an intermediate temperature to see if the 3/4 pair can be nudged above 1.5 without lengthening the run as much as at 25 C. This is the best chance to beat the current CRF by trading a small selectivity shift for less time penalty.

The critical overlap shifts markedly with temperature: 25 C gives a near miss at 3/4, while 30 C creates a bad 2/3 overlap. Testing 35 C maps that selectivity trend on the way to 40 C and may reveal a temperature where all pairs are acceptable with less retention than at 25 C.

The best region is clearly around 25 C, and only a small amount of extra resolution is missing at tG=20. Try a slightly shorter gradient to see whether the selectivity pattern remains favorable while pulling t_last closer to 10 min; if resolution drops too much, we know injection 6 is already near-optimal.

Use 25 C, where selectivity is best, and increase tG one more step beyond 22 min to confirm the fully resolved region and see whether extra margin appears in the critical pairs. This sacrifices some CRF if successful, but it maps the resolution-vs-slope boundary at the best temperature so later optimization can safely shorten around it.

The broad-window temperature sweep shows strong reordering/selectivity changes, but only up to 40 C so far. Test 45 C to complete that trend and check whether the critical overlap continues moving in a way that might allow all pairs to clear 1.5 with a shorter run than at 25 C.

At 45 C the run is fast and only modestly under-resolved, so a small increase in tG may lift both subcritical pairs above 1.5 while likely keeping t_last close enough to 10 min to challenge the current best. This directly tests whether the high-temperature branch can outperform the 25 C method on speed.

The best method is still 20 min at 25 C, but we have not yet mapped the immediate tG step above 24 min at that temperature where pair identities appear to shift. Testing 26 min will clarify whether a different pair becomes limiting and whether there is any unexpected selectivity sweet spot near the full-resolution boundary.

The most promising unexplored axis is still temperature above 45 C, where retention is shorter and the limiting pairs differ from those at 25 C. A 50 C run will show whether the fast branch can recover enough selectivity to exceed the current best while keeping t_last safely under 10 min.

One last endpoint on temperature will complete the selectivity map and confirm whether the high-temperature region is definitively worse or if another reordering emerges. This closes out the broad temperature screen before focusing the remaining budget on fine optimization around the 25 C optimum.

At 60 C the run is fastest and only one pair is modestly below 1.5, making this the strongest route to a better CRF. A small increase in tG should selectively open that remaining pair while likely keeping t_last near or below 10 min.

The 60 C branch is best, and increasing tG made the limiting pair worse, so the pair is not helped by shallower slope. Try a slightly steeper gradient to see if that critical 5/6 pair opens further while still keeping all peaks comfortably before 10 min.

At 60 C, making the gradient steeper improved the limiting pair and gave an almost perfect score, so test one more step steeper to see if that last near-critical pair crosses 1.5 while all peaks remain well before 10 min. This is the most direct path to CRF 1.0.

The optimum is very sharp around 18 min at high temperature, and 60 C is just barely limited by one pair. Test 55 C at the same tG to see if a small temperature decrease improves that last critical separation while keeping t_last comfortably under 10 min.

Use the remaining budget to probe whether temperature, not slope, is the fine control around the near-optimal 18 min condition. A lower temperature could shift the critical pair just enough to clear 1.5 while still keeping the last peak under 10 min.

The best method is nearly perfect and all peaks elute well after the dead time, so a small increase in phi0 may shorten the early part of the run without sacrificing the critical selectivity. This tests whether the same high score can be maintained with an even more time-efficient gradient shape.

Keep the near-optimal 18 min, 60 C condition but slightly narrow the gradient from the high-organic end rather than raising phi0, since all analytes elute well before the late hold. This may redistribute gradient strength in the active elution region and lift the remaining near-critical pair over 1.5.

Further narrow the high-organic end at the best slope and temperature, since reducing phi1 from 0.95 to 0.90 preserved a near-perfect score and changed which pair was limiting. This may place the active elution region in a slightly more favorable part of the gradient and give the remaining small resolution gain to reach 1.0.

For the last shot, combine the two mild window trims that each stayed close to optimal but shifted which pair was limiting. This may redistribute selectivity in the central elution region enough to push the remaining near-critical pair over 1.5 while keeping the run very short.
